maluku-sez-maes-inkiene-demolition.whole: By the completion report's count 211 hectares of land at Maluku were secured by the government and developed for industrial use, with a protective wall 6,155 metres long built around them with project money; the agency for special economic zones was set up and made operational, a consultant consortium was hired to draft the regulations implementing the 2015 zone law and to update the demand study, and a private developer was selected from seven respondents with the public-private partnership signed at the end of January 2020. The report gives two accounts of the resettlement. In one, the land was acquired under Bank policies, a resettlement action plan was fully implemented and some 300 land concession holders were compensated. In the other, poor implementation of that plan, together with the absence of an environmental and social management plan for a wholesale market the government built inside the zone, led the Bank to suspend disbursements for the zone component for 14.5 months, from a notice of 13 January 2016 to March 2017: the joint-venture company had already begun building an access road, power supply and port works before the safeguards requirements were met, and the suspension was lifted once the owner of its land had been compensated and a management plan prepared. The report rates environmental and social safeguards Moderately Satisfactory for that reason, records that the government paid US$4,422,055.68 to 622 people listed in the project area, and says that of 49 complaints from vegetable growers in the zone in September 2018, 37 people were found eligible for compensation and received it. After the mid-term review the infrastructure to be financed was cut: basic infrastructure for an initial 59 hectares was dropped, leaving the government and the developer to pay for the physical works needed, and the component's allocation fell from US$27 million at appraisal to US$6 million. The agro-industrial parks in the project were cut from three to one. On the agricultural side the project rehabilitated 542 kilometres of rural road against a target of 500 and recorded 97,757 direct beneficiaries against a target of 50,000, 44 per cent of them women against a 40 per cent target. Jobs created in the selected value chains came to 5,026 against 11,000 at appraisal and a target cut to 5,000 at the 2018 restructuring, with women 19 per cent of them against a 50 per cent target. Yields were 3.1 tonnes a hectare for rice against a target of 3, 10 tonnes for palm oil against 15 at appraisal and a revised 10, and 18.4 tonnes for cassava against 20, which the report attributes partly to improved varieties already in use before the project and to growers keeping old varieties alongside new ones. The three production volumes are printed on two scales: the framework gives 1,325.86 tonnes of cassava against 3,900 at appraisal and a revised 2,500, 35.4 tonnes of rice against 37 and a revised 25, and 113,656 tonnes of palm oil against 750 and a revised 450, while the report's comments on the same rows give each figure multiplied by a thousand; on either scale cassava reached 53 per cent of its revised target, rice 142 per cent and palm oil 25,257 per cent. The three revised volume targets were agreed at the mid-term review but, the report says, were left out of the January 2018 restructuring and only recorded in July 2019. Processed food came to 163,861.53 tonnes against 5,000 at appraisal and a target cut to 1,000. Collection centres, including parking and warehouses, were not built, the report citing cost, difficulties over access to land and the time left to do the works. The report puts the economic rate of return at 21.9 per cent at completion against 32.4 per cent at appraisal, with a net present value of US$33.7 million, a benefit-cost ratio of 1.55 and a financial return of 21.3 per cent, and says a two-year delay in benefits would bring the rate to 11 per cent, below the 12 per cent opportunity cost of capital; it also records cost overruns and a foreign exchange loss of about US$7 million. The report rates efficiency Substantial while the Evaluation Group's review rates it Modest. All these figures are the lender's own; no check from outside the World Bank Group was found.
maluku-sez-maes-inkiene-demolition.why: Checked against ICR00005497 (Annex 1 row by row, Table 3, paragraphs 20, 35, 43-51, 77-81, footnotes 10 and 18) and ICRR0022662 in full. Ruling on the three volume rows: they are kept, because the ratios are internally consistent on either scale - 1,325.86/2,500 is 53 per cent, 35.4/25 is 142 per cent and 113,656/450 is 25,257 per cent, exactly as the report's comments compute them after multiplying both sides by a thousand - so the earlier statement that the percentages could not be reconciled was wrong; what cannot be settled from the document is which scale is meant, and the palm oil row is implausible on either. The row comments also record that the three revised targets were agreed at the mid-term review and only formally captured in July 2019. On the resettlement tension, paragraphs 77 and 81 are now set against paragraph 35: 'poor implementation of the RAP for the SEZ of Maluku and the absence of an ESMP linked to the construction by the government of a wholesale market within the zone resulted in the WB's management decision to partially suspend disbursements', notified 13 January 2016 and lifted March 2017, with the works launched before the requirements were met; paragraph 77 gives the US$4,422,055.68 paid to 622 people and paragraph 79 the 49 vegetable-grower complaints with 37 compensated. Added from paragraphs 50-51: the agro-industrial parks cut from three to one and the US$7 million exchange loss; paragraph 49 gives 11 per cent as the rate under a two-year delay.

freetown-wellington-33kv-demolitions.whole: The project replaced and upgraded the 7.8 kilometre line from the Blackhall Road substation to Wellington by way of the Ropoti substation, from 11 kV to 33 kV on double-circuit towers, against a target of 7.5 kilometres, and rehabilitated five substations against a target of four: Wilberforce, Kingtom, Blackhall Road, Ropoti and Wellington, Ropoti being new, while Blackhall Road was only rehabilitated and its new equipment was left to be installed under another Bank project. It installed 20,000 prepaid meters, 17,800 single-phase and 2,200 three-phase, in 20 neighbourhoods of Freetown, its target, and 100 bulk meters at eight switching stations and substations against a target of 200, from a baseline of 80. Losses in the project area fell from 38 per cent to 34.5 per cent against a target of 33, which the completion report calls 70 per cent of the target, describes as preliminary and dates to September 2016, ten months before closing; the distribution utility's collection rate rose from 76 per cent to 86, its target, which the report attributes to more prepaid than postpaid customers and to a revenue protection and arrears recovery programme; and 720,000 people were counted as beneficiaries against 205,400 at appraisal and a revised 624,000, a figure derived from 120,000 households connected during implementation at six people a household. The project management unit hired six staff against seven planned and a revised four, the report adding that their technical capacity needed improvement. The rural electrification component was cancelled at the October 2015 restructuring and the third objective, increasing access to electricity in selected rural areas, was removed from the project: none of the 28 photovoltaic systems for public buildings in rural villages was installed, and that indicator was dropped at the same time. The report puts the economic rate of return at 14 per cent at completion against 39 per cent at appraisal, with a net present value of US$2.46 million over a 20-year life against US$26.7 million at appraisal, and the financial return at 33 per cent against 36 per cent with a net present value of US$23.43 million against US$11.3 million, and says the economic returns are moderate because the loss reduction investments return relatively little. Both the report and the Evaluation Group's review rate efficiency Modest. Implementation was delayed before the Ebola outbreak by the unit's limited capacity in procurement and safeguards and nearly stopped during it, with supervision missions at times moved to Abidjan, which the report says made a realistic assessment of problems on the ground impossible. All these figures are the lender's own; no check from outside the World Bank Group was found.

laulara-solerema-road-structures.whole: The project rehabilitated the Dili to Ainaro corridor in five lots totalling about 109 kilometres, and by the completion report's count drainage in good condition on the corridor reached 99.96 per cent against 20 per cent at appraisal and a target raised to 90 per cent in 2017, roads in good or fair condition 99.63 per cent against a baseline of 10, 50 per cent at appraisal and a revised 90, road roughness fell to 3.43 metres per kilometre from a baseline of 9 against 6.5 at appraisal and a revised 3.5 - an average of Lots 1, 2 and 3 only - and slope protection was improved at 1,350 locations against 25 at appraisal and a revised 820, including 352 of 362 stone masonry retaining walls and all 141 gabions. Incidents needing emergency repairs on the corridor fell from 53 a year to three - a tree falling on a house in April 2022 and two fatal incidents in August and September 2022 - against 30 at appraisal and a revised 15, the unit of that indicator having changed from a percentage to a count of incidents. Traffic grew 250 per cent against a 30 per cent target, from 835 vehicles a day in 2014 to 2,926 in 2023 on the corridor count, while the report's economic analysis gives 3,048 vehicles a day in 2014 and 10,741 in 2023 at the Dili count station. Of 53 grievances recorded by 22 November 2022, four concerned environment, health and safety, 43 social matters and six resettlement, all of them on Lot 2, and all were answered within the service standard except one settled after three months. Lot 2, the Laulara to Solerema section, stood at 93.94 per cent on the second variation order and was taken over at 97.28 per cent of its as-built value, US$16,542,026.34, with US$462,737.61 of work outstanding on force majeure grounds and 22.21 kilometres paved, and its four-year performance-based maintenance contract was to start in June 2024; multi-year performance-based maintenance covered 79 per cent of the corridor, Lots 1, 3, 4 and 5, whose two-year contracts ended between July 2019 and February 2022. Three maintenance sub-components were cancelled when the 2013 additional financing extended the works to the whole corridor, with routine maintenance and emergency response written into the civil works contracts instead, and the emergency planning and response sub-component was cancelled at the 2017 restructuring; the component for feasibility studies and detailed designs, which at appraisal named five road segments linked to the corridor, was narrowed in 2017 to selected segments, and the procurement of two detailed engineering design packages was cancelled. The report puts the economic rate of return at 21.4 per cent at completion with a net present value of US$59.40 million, against 18 per cent and US$2.07 million at appraisal, 14 per cent and US$13.51 million at the 2013 additional financing and 15.9 per cent and US$30.01 million at the 2017 one, and attributes the rise mainly to Lot 2's cost falling from US$26.835 million to US$18.235 million and to higher traffic. It attributes the delays to the government's reprioritisation of Lot 2, the departure of all the project unit's international consultants in December 2018, Tropical Cyclone Seroja in 2021 and the pandemic. The report rates efficiency Substantial; the Evaluation Group's review rates it Modest, on an implementation period of more than ten years with seven years of extensions, project implementation support costs rising from under US$1 million at appraisal to US$3.04 million, and a reduced scope for maintenance, institutional development and community engagement. All these figures are the lender's own; no check from outside the World Bank Group was found.

nigeria-federal-roads-trader-relocations.whole: The project rehabilitated 300 kilometres of federal road against a target of 442 - a figure the completion report's own key-outputs table gives as 310 - completing all 121 kilometres of the Mokwa to Bida road, 72 of 77 kilometres from Enugu to Abakaliki, 65 of 74 kilometres from Akure to Ilesha and 52 of 53 kilometres from Ogoja Junction to Ikom, while the 117 kilometre Gombe to Biu road was dropped for want of funds, the Evaluation Group's review adding that contract prices from the bidding method adopted after the original output-based bidding failed came in higher than the appraisal estimates. It upgraded or maintained 288 kilometres against 340 planned, across 14 sections: four were delivered in full or beyond - Takai to Albasu to Gaya in Kano, both sections of Ado Ilumoba to Agbado to Ikare in Ekiti, Akure to Owo to Ifo in Ondo and East-West to Odi in Bayelsa - while the largest shortfalls were 17.5 of 48 kilometres from Hong to Mubi, 11.5 of 23 kilometres from Lafiagi to Mokwa, 9.1 of 16.5 kilometres from Rumukurushi to Chokocho, 22 of 28 from Kurfi to Charanchi, 20.8 of 25 from Lafia to Doma and 22 of 24 from Jebba to Lafiagi. Six pedestrian overbridges were built, the target, which the report says about 12,000 pedestrians a day use; the safe corridor approach was applied on four of five corridors, the fifth dropped for want of funds; the HDM-4 road model was calibrated for Nigeria and national road design standards were put in place, though the report notes axle load standards are not. Average travel time on the project roads fell from 120 to 60 minutes per 100 kilometres against a target of 90 cut to 80, average vehicle operating costs from 40 to 38 US cents a vehicle-kilometre, the target, and the report adds that passenger fares fell by up to 30 per cent and truck rates by up to 15 per cent on the rehabilitated roads. Two outcome rows fell short: the fatality rate was 143 deaths per 10,000 vehicles against a target of 120 from a baseline of 161, which the report calls an 11 per cent fall against the 25 per cent intended, and direct project beneficiaries came to 340,000 against 500,000, which the report ties to the shorter lengths of road built. The road sector database held 3,000 of the 10,000 kilometres targeted and the asset management system covered 3,000 of 6,800 kilometres. The report puts the economic rate of return on the rehabilitated roads at 58.08 per cent at completion against 53 per cent in the November 2010 estimate, with the present value of net benefits at US$821.81 million against US$169 million, and on the roads given upgrading or periodic maintenance at 47.59 per cent against 46 per cent, with net benefits of US$251.19 million against US$146 million, covering 77 per cent of total project cost; it rates efficiency Substantial. The review rates efficiency Modest, on long delays, significant cost increases and the downsizing of the project's scope, and notes the project closed six months late. All these figures are the lender's own; no check from outside the World Bank Group was found.
nigeria-federal-roads-trader-relocations.why: Checked against ICR00004170 (Annex 1 row by row, the key-outputs tables road by road, paragraphs 40-41 with Table 2) and ICRR0021110 in full. Corrections: the upgrading and periodic maintenance list runs to 14 sections, and the earlier text named seven, leaving out Lafiagi-Mokwa at 11.5 of 23 km (50 per cent), Lafia-Doma at 20.8 of 25 km and Dingaya-Galambi-Rungo at 16.7 of 18.5 km as well as the over-delivered sections, so the whole list is now summarised with the four full or over-delivered sections named; paragraph 40 adds the fall in passenger fares and truck rates; the 53 and 46 per cent rates are labelled in the report's own table as ex ante November 2010, and the review says they come from a fresh analysis at the February 2011 restructuring after the output and performance based bidding failed, so the date rather than 'appraisal' is used. The travel-time row's unit column says hours while the indicator's name says minutes per 100 km; the name is used, since 120 hours per 100 km is impossible. The Okpala-Igwurita row, printed as 24 km completed against 18.2 km planned and 76 per cent achieved, cannot be read consistently and is still left out.

addo-park-farm-worker-rehousing.whole: By the completion report's count the protected terrestrial area around the park grew from 141,000 hectares to 170,115, against 236,000 planned at appraisal and a target cut to 205,000 in September 2007, which the report calls 83 per cent achieved. Of the marine area, 7,414 hectares were declared, Bird Island and St Croix, with the 120,000 hectares of the planned marine protected area submitted and awaiting final approval at closing. Private land brought into the park through conservation partnerships came to 17,608 hectares against 46,000 at appraisal and a target cut to 30,000, which the report calls 59 per cent achieved, with a further 11,000 hectares of community land awaiting incorporation by the Enon Bersheba communities trust, the report saying land titling questions proved more complicated than expected. Wildlife was fenced within 133,000 hectares against a target of 130,000, alien species were cleared from 75,044 hectares against 65,000, a monitoring and management information system was built whose environmental component was later used in 22 other parks, 11 small enterprises with more than three permanent employees and two years of trading were created against a target of 10, three partnership agreements were signed and six commercial concessions were operating, all targets, and an environmental education centre was built that the report says about 12,806 primary and secondary school students visit a year. Employment in the greater park area rose to 1,842 people against a target of 1,596, from a baseline the report's framework gives as 1,228 and the Evaluation Group's review as 909, and the review adds 434 jobs inside the park administration against 106 at the start; 514 training days a year were delivered against 350, and 32 learnerships and internships against 30. Tourist entries rose from 94,699 in 2004 to 135,109 in 2010, against 180,000 at appraisal and a revised target of 120,000, and tourist accommodation went from 174 beds to 505. The park's revenue covered 132 per cent of the cost of managing it in 2009/10, against 94.6 per cent at the project's start, making it one of the few parks in South Africa whose revenue exceeds its operating costs, and the government's counterpart funding rose from US$28 million to US$54 million. No economic or financial rate of return was calculated at appraisal or at completion, the report saying such calculations were not required for a stand-alone grant of this kind and would be very hard to produce after the event. Both the completion report and the review rate efficiency Substantial, and the review rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory against the report's Satisfactory, on the ground that the data do not show how far poverty was reduced: there are no figures in the report on changes in tourism revenues or on how many people moved out of marginal traditional farming into better paid tourism work. The review also notes there is no information on how the unit costs of the infrastructure built compare with similar projects. All these figures are the lender's own; no check from outside the World Bank Group was found.
